note: Matthew 12:27 ('your sons' cast out demons) and Acts 19:13 both attest Jewish exorcists in the period; Acts adds itinerant exorcists invoking the name of Jesus.
The excavated city site is identified with Ephesus itself; a source names the place ('city on the coast of Ionia, in present-day Selçuk in İzmir Province, Turkey').
The excavated city confirms the Ephesus of Acts 19 as a real, major Ionian city (the setting of the claim); it does not attest Paul's arrival itself.
The excavated Artemision at Ephesus, one of the Seven Wonders, names and locates the very temple the town clerk's speech defends; rediscovered in 1869 by John Turtle Wood.
The Artemision was the cult center whose prestige a Claudian edict presupposes; it confirms the Artemis cult's standing in the same city and period.

The excavated Great Theatre of Ephesus (estimated 25,000 seats, the largest in the ancient world) is the assembly venue named in Acts 19:29; the fetched Riot in Ephesus article confirms the theater's role as the citizen assembly's meeting place. Regraded A to B by the architect: the theatre is the excavated assembly venue, but the rush of the crowd is not attested. Split per the architect's titles/offices ruling: the building-grade A now anchors claim:ac-19-29-theater-venue; this edge keeps B for the event.

Surviving 1st-2nd century statues of the Ephesian goddess (Ephesus Archaeological Museum, Naples) document the same goddess and her cult in the same period, including beyond Ephesus (Farnese Artemis, Naples).

An Ephesian inscription naming 'the association of silversmiths' (to synderion ton argyrokopon) confirms the silversmith trade of Acts 19:24 in the same city; it does not name Demetrius or the shrines.

The inscription confirms a silversmiths' guild existed at Ephesus (the trade Acts attributes to Demetrius); Demetrius himself is not externally attested, and 'no shrines of the kind attributed to Demetrius have been discovered'.

The 104 CE Salutaris foundation funded silver images of Artemis carried in procession from her temple to the theatre - the same city, cult and silver-artwork practice fifty years after Acts 19 (grade per the seed lead; the gap is noted).

The decree schedules the silver images to be carried to the theatre 'during the twelve sacred and regular assembly meetings fixed by law and custom' - direct evidence for Ephesus's regular lawful assembly (ennomosekklesia) of Acts 19:39.
The foundation's parade carried the silver images from the temple of Artemis to the theatre, confirming the theatre's civic-assembly and festival role in Ephesus.

An edict issued at Ephesus by Paullus Fabius Persicus, proconsul of Asia, under Claudius names the office in the same city and period: 'The province of Asia was, as a rule, governed by proconsuls staying in office only a year.' Regraded A to B (reviewer 11, architect's titles/offices ruling): the edict is A for the proconsular office and its one-year tenure, now anchored on claim:ac-19-38-proconsul-office; it is B for the courts-open event.

A 2nd-century proconsular edict from nearby Magnesia records a guild riot using words for disturbance, tumult and sedition closely resembling Acts 19's vocabulary - a later, neighboring parallel for the charge the Ephesian clerk feared.
The edict is itself a proconsular judgment arising from a guild riot in the same province, illustrating the legal channel Acts 19:38 points to (parallel from a later decade).

The Martyrdom of Polycarp (12.2) mentions Asiarchs at Polycarp's trial in Smyrna a century after Acts 19 - literary confirmation that the office continued and functioned in the cities of Asia; the fetched Asiarch article cites it alongside Acts 19:31. Moved to the office claim in the split (the evidence is about the office, not the urging).
Dio Chrysostom, a contemporary, describes guild-driven civic unrest among the linen workers of Tarsus in comparable language - a first-century parallel from another Asia Minor city.

Josephus saw Eleazar release the possessed in the presence of Vespasian using incantations - evidence for Jewish exorcism as a known practice in the same era (a Jewish practice in a different setting; the Ephesian episode itself is unattested externally).

Plutarch reports that Magi instructed those believed to be possessed to recite the Ephesian letters - literary evidence that Ephesian magical formulas were a known remedy for possession in the period.

The six-word Ephesian magical formula is attested epigraphically from Himera, Sicily, before 409 BC, and reappears on magical papyri through the Hellenistic period - the tradition behind 'books of magic' at Ephesus, though the find is earlier and elsewhere.

Numerous inscriptions name Asiarchs of the province of Asia, elected by the cities and confirmed by the Roman proconsul; the fetched article states they are 'known from numerous inscriptions, but are also mentioned in Acts (19:31)'. The identity of Asiarchs with the high priests of Asia is disputed in research; the existence of the office is not. Regraded A to B by the architect: the inscriptions name the office of Asiarch (A for the office), but not Asiarchs befriending Paul. Split per the architect's titles/offices ruling: the office-grade A now anchors claim:ac-19-31-asiarch-office; this edge keeps B for the event.

Ephesian official documents were dated by the grammateus, whose office was 'among the most prominent in Ephesus'; the Salutaris decree was likewise introduced by the grammateus tou demou, 'an officer with ample political influence in the imperial period'. Regraded A to B by the architect: the inscriptions name the office of grammateus at Ephesus (A for the office), but not the clerk's quieting of the crowd. Split per the architect's titles/offices ruling: the office-grade A now anchors claim:ac-19-35-grammateus-office; this edge keeps B for the event.

Ephesus's own civic coins title the city neokoros ('four times neokoros'), naming the same office and city; the article states the title for Ephesus as guardian of the Artemision 'is attested in inscriptions and on coins'. The illustrated coin is Elagabalus-era and its four neocorates are the later imperial ones; the Artemis title is the older usage. Regraded A to B (reviewer 11, architect's titles/offices ruling): the coin evidence is A for the city's neokoros title alone, now anchored on claim:ac-19-35-neokoros-title; it is B for the speech claim.

Roman decrees reported by Josephus confirm Jews were settled at Ephesus and observed their religious rites there in the late Republic (Roman citizens who 'follow the Jewish religious rites, and yet live at Ephesus'), the community whose synagogue Acts 19:8 presupposes; no synagogue building of Acts 19:8 is known.
The excavated city is the Ephesus of Acts 19; it confirms the setting, not the three-month synagogue preaching itself.
The excavated site at Selçuk is ancient Ephesus; the city moved location as the harbour silted, but the identification is not disputed.
The Artemision stood in the territory of Ephesus, near modern Selçuk; identified without dispute (UNESCO World Heritage listing within Ephesus).
The Great Theatre is part of the excavated Ephesus site; identified without dispute.
